Empirical Research Plan – “School Spending & Educational Outcomes, 1990-2015”

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered treatment timing, complemented by an event-study and an instrumented DID (2SLS) that uses exogenous, formula-driven funding shocks.

Why DID is appropriate  
• 1990-2015 panel of districts → rich pre/post variation.  
• Exogenous shifts in funding arise from state court rulings or legislative formula changes that apply to all districts in a state but bite differentially depending on observable pre-reform characteristics (e.g., low local revenue capacity).  
• These shocks are plausibly orthogonal to district-specific latent trends in achievement once we absorb district and year fixed effects and control for demographics.  

Why augment with IV  
• Endogeneity remains if districts can change tax effort in response to state aid.  
• We build a “Bartik-style” instrument: Post-reform × (pre-reform state-aid share). This isolates mechanically induced spending changes, not districts’ voluntary spending.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
spend_pc_it: Total instructional expenditure per pupil in district i, year t (real $, 2015 CPI).

Definition of “treated” in DID framework  
A treated observation is any district-year after its state’s funding reform takes effect. Districts in non-reform states or pre-reform years are controls.

Treatment timing / event date  
For every state s we code reform_yr_s = first fiscal year in which the new formula or court-ordered funding is implemented. The treatment indicator:

treated_it = 1{state_i reform implemented by year t}.

Event time k = t − reform_yr_s used for dynamic effects.

Control group  
Districts in states that have not yet reformed (or never reform during sample) in that calendar year provide the counterfactual trend.

Instrument (for 2SLS)  
Z_it = treated_it × pre_stateaidshare_i, where pre_stateaidshare_i = average (1987-1989) share of revenue from state aid. Intuition: districts initially more dependent on state aid receive mechanically larger dollar increases when the state raises per-pupil aid.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends (DID): In absence of reform, achievement trends would have been the same across soon-to-be-treated and never-treated districts.  
Plausibility: Court rulings are triggered by constitutional equity concerns, not contemporaneous achievement dips. Will test in pre-period event-study.

A2. No anticipation: Districts do not significantly change spending or test preparation in advance of a reform they cannot perfectly predict.  
Court rulings often come with short implementation lags; anticipate but check pre-period coefficients.

A3. Stable composition: No systematic district boundary changes or selective school closings correlated with reform.  
Will verify using enrollment counts and district IDs.

A4. Exogenous instrument (2SLS only): Pre-reform state-aid share is pre-determined and uncorrelated with post-1990 shocks to achievement, conditional on controls.  
Plausible: share measured well before reforms; include state × year FE to net out state-wide shocks.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in TWFE.  
Remedy: Use Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) group-specific DID estimator and Goodman-Bacon decomposition to show weights are benign. Provide robustness with Sun & Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted event-study.

T2. Concurrent policy changes (e.g., accountability laws, class-size mandates).  
Remedy: Control for state-year policy dummies; drop states with major overlapping reforms in robustness; include state-specific linear time trends.

T3. Endogenous local tax changes (“crowd-out”).  
Remedy: 2SLS specification with formula-driven instrument; also examine differential effects on state aid vs. local spending components separately.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast two-way FE & IV
library(did)          # Callaway-Sant'Anna estimator
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load data ---------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("district_panel_1990_2015.csv")   # district-year panel

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------
dt[, year := as.integer(year)]
dt[, l_spend_pc := log(spend_per_pupil_real)]

# Treatment variables
state_reform_years <- fread("state_reform_years.csv")  # state, reform_yr
dt <- merge(dt, state_reform_years, by = "state")

dt[, treated := as.integer(year >= reform_yr)]
dt[, event_time := year - reform_yr]        # negative pre, 0 first treated yr

# Instrument
pre_aid <- dt[year %in% 1987:1989,
              .(pre_stateaid = mean(state_aid_share, na.rm=TRUE)), 
              by = district_id]
dt <- merge(dt, pre_aid, by = "district_id", all.x = TRUE)
dt[, Z := treated * pre_stateaid]

# 3. Main TWFE DID ----------------------------------------------
did_twfe <- feols(test_score_std ~ treated + 
                    district_demographics + 
                    fe(district_id) + fe(year), 
                  data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham) -------------------------------
event <- sunab(dt$reform_yr, dt$year)
event_model <- feols(test_score_std ~ event + district_demographics | 
                     district_id + year, data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 5. IV specification -------------------------------------------
iv_mod <- feols(test_score_std ~ 1 | district_id + year | 
                l_spend_pc ~ Z,        # 2SLS
                data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 6. Callaway-Sant’Anna DID -------------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname = "test_score_std",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "district_id",
             gname = "reform_yr",
             xformla = ~ district_demographics,
             data = dt)
agg_effect <- aggte(cs, type = "group")

# 7. Robustness: add state-specific trends ----------------------
dt[, state_year := interaction(state, year)]
trend_mod <- feols(test_score_std ~ treated + district_demographics | 
                   district_id + state_year, data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 8. Display -----------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(DID = did_twfe, IV = iv_mod, Trend = trend_mod),
             statistic = "({stat})", stars = TRUE)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (education production function) and prior empirical work suggest positive, diminishing-returns effects. I expect:

• A $1,000 (2015$) increase in per-pupil spending raises average math/reading scores by ~0.04–0.07 SD within four years.  
• Larger gains for low-income and minority students; long-run outcomes (graduation, earnings) likely improve proportionately (~1–2 % increase in high-school graduation rate per $1,000).

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends – 0.8  
C2: No anticipation – 0.7  
C3: Stable composition – 0.9  
C4: Exogenous treatment timing – 0.7  
C5: No spillovers (SUTVA) – 0.6  

(1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = mostly, 0 = doubtful)

Overall, assumptions are plausible but require empirical verification through the diagnostics and robustness exercises described above.
